{{Short description|Probability distribution}}
[[File:Tracy-Widom distr.svg|thumb|right|300px|Densities of Tracy–Widom distributions for ''β''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;4]]
The '''Tracy–Widom distribution''' is a [[probability distribution]] from [[random matrix|random matrix theory]] introduced by {{harvs |first1=Craig |last1=Tracy |author1-link=Craig Tracy (mathematician) |first2=Harold |last2=Widom |author2-link=Harold Widom |year1=1993 |year2=1994 |txt}}. It is the distribution of the normalized largest [[eigenvalue]] of a [[Gaussian unitary ensemble|random]] [[Hermitian matrix]]. The distribution is defined as a [[Fredholm determinant]].

In practical terms, Tracy–Widom is the crossover function between the two phases of weakly versus strongly coupled components in a system.<ref>[https://www.wired.com/2014/10/tracy-widom-mysterious-statistical-law/ ''Mysterious Statistical Law May Finally Have an Explanation''], wired.com 2014-10-27</ref>
It also appears in the distribution of the length of the [[longest increasing subsequence]] of random [[permutation]]s,{{sfnp|Baik|Deift|Johansson|1999}} as large-scale statistics in the [[Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Sasamoto|Spohn|2010}}</ref> in current fluctuations of the [[asymmetric simple exclusion process]] (ASEP) with step initial condition,<ref>{{harvtxt|Johansson|2000}}; {{harvtxt|Tracy|Widom|2009}}).</ref> and in simplified mathematical models of the behavior of the [[longest common subsequence]] problem on random inputs.{{sfnp|Majumdar|Nechaev|2005}} See {{harvtxt|Takeuchi|Sano|2010}} and {{harvtxt|Takeuchi|Sano|Sasamoto|Spohn|2011}} for experimental testing (and verifying) that the interface fluctuations of a growing droplet (or substrate) are described by the TW distribution <math> F_2</math> (or <math>F_1</math>) as predicted by {{harvtxt|Prähofer|Spohn|2000}}.

The distribution <math>F_1</math> is of particular interest in [[multivariate statistics]].<ref>{{harvs|last=Johnstone|year=2007|year2=2008|year3=2009|txt}}.</ref> For a discussion of the universality of <math>F_\beta</math>, <math>\beta=1,2,4</math>, see {{harvtxt|Deift|2007}}. For an application of <math>F_1</math> to inferring population structure from genetic data see {{harvtxt|Patterson|Price|Reich|2006}}.
In 2017 it was proved that the distribution F is not infinitely divisible.{{sfnp|Domínguez-Molina|2017}}

==Definition as a law of large numbers==
[[File:Tracy–Widom distribution of the largest eigenvalue of Gaussian ensembles.png|thumb|The empirical distribution of the largest eigenvalue of matrices sampled from the Gaussian ensembles, for increasingly large matrix sizes. They converge to their respective Tracy–Widom distributions.]]
Let <math>F_\beta</math> denote the [[cumulative distribution function]] of the Tracy–Widom distribution with given <math>\beta</math>. It can be defined as a law of large numbers, similar to the [[central limit theorem]].

There are typically three Tracy–Widom distributions, <math>F_\beta</math>, with <math>\beta \in \{1, 2, 4\}</math>. They correspond to the three [[Random matrix#Gaussian ensembles|gaussian ensembles]]: orthogonal (<math>\beta=1</math>), unitary (<math>\beta=2</math>), and symplectic (<math>\beta=4</math>). However, the Tracy–Widom distribution family allows arbitrary <math>\beta > 0</math>, though the cases other than <math>\beta = 1, 2, 4, 6</math> are not known to be solvable by Painlevé transcendents.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Majumdar |first1=Satya N. |last2=Pal |first2=Arnab |last3=Schehr |first3=Grégory |date=2020-01-22 |title=Extreme value statistics of correlated random variables: A pedagogical review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370157319303291 |journal=Physics Reports |volume=840 |pages=1–32 |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2019.10.005 |arxiv=1910.10667 |bibcode=2020PhR...840....1M |issn=0370-1573}}</ref>

In general, consider a gaussian ensemble with beta value <math>\beta</math>, with its diagonal entries having variance 1, and off-diagonal entries having variance <math>\sigma^2</math>, and let <math>F_{N, \beta}(s)</math> be probability that an <math>N\times N</math> matrix sampled from the ensemble have maximal eigenvalue <math>\leq s</math>, then define<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Tracy |first1=Craig A. |last2=Widom |first2=Harold |title=New Trends in Mathematical Physics |chapter=The Distributions of Random Matrix Theory and their Applications |date=2009b |editor-last=Sidoravičius |editor-first=Vladas |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-90-481-2810-5_48 |language=en |location=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |pages=753–765 |doi=10.1007/978-90-481-2810-5_48 |isbn=978-90-481-2810-5}}</ref><math display="block">F_\beta(x) = \lim_{N\to \infty} F_{N, \beta}(\sigma(2N^{1/2} + N^{-1/6} x)) =\lim_{N \to \infty} \operatorname{Pr}(N^{1/6}(\lambda_{\max}/\sigma - 2N^{1/2}) \leq x)</math>where <math>\lambda_{\max}</math> denotes the largest eigenvalue of the random matrix. The shift by <math>2\sigma N^{1/2}</math> centers the distribution, since at the limit, the eigenvalue distribution converges to the semicircular distribution with radius <math>2\sigma N^{1/2}</math>. The multiplication by <math>N^{1/6}</math> is used because the standard deviation of the distribution scales as <math>N^{-1/6}</math> (first derived in <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Forrester |first=P. J. |date=1993-08-09 |title=The spectrum edge of random matrix ensembles |journal=Nuclear Physics B |language=en |volume=402 |issue=3 |pages=709–728 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(93)90126-A |bibcode=1993NuPhB.402..709F |issn=0550-3213}}</ref>).

For example:{{sfnp|Tracy|Widom|1996}}
:<math>F_2(x) = \lim_{N\to \infty} \operatorname{Prob}\left( (\lambda_{\max}-\sqrt{4N})N^{1/6}\leq x\right),</math>

where the matrix is sampled from the gaussian unitary ensemble with off-diagonal variance <math>1</math>.

The definition of the Tracy–Widom distributions <math>F_\beta</math> may be extended to all <math>\beta >0</math> (Slide 56 in {{harvtxt|Edelman|2003}}, {{harvtxt|Ramírez|Rider| Virág|2006}}).

One may naturally ask for the limit distribution of second-largest eigenvalues, third-largest eigenvalues, etc. They are known.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dieng |first=Momar |date=2005 |title=Distribution functions for edge eigenvalues in orthogonal and symplectic ensembles: Painlevé representations |journal=International Mathematics Research Notices |volume=2005 |issue=37 |pages=2263–2287 |doi=10.1155/IMRN.2005.2263 |issn=1687-0247 |doi-access=<!-- not free-->}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

For heavy-tailed random matrices,<ref>{{Citation |last1=Burda |first1=Zdzislaw |chapter=Heavy-tailed random matrices |date=2015-09-17 |title=The Oxford Handbook of Random Matrix Theory |pages=270–289 |editor-last=Akemann |editor-first=Gernot |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-874419-1 |last2=Jurkiewicz |first2=Jerzy |doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198744191.013.13 |editor2-last=Baik |editor2-first=Jinho |editor3-last=Di Francesco |editor3-first=Philippe}}</ref> the extreme eigenvalue distribution is modified.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Biroli |first1=G |last2=Bouchaud |first2=J.-P |last3=Potters |first3=M |date=April 2007 |title=On the top eigenvalue of heavy-tailed random matrices |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/78/10001 |journal=Europhysics Letters |volume=78 |issue=1 |article-number=10001 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/78/10001 |arxiv=cond-mat/0609070 |bibcode=2007EL.....7810001B |issn=0295-5075}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Auffinger |first1=Antonio |last2=Ben Arous |first2=Gérard |last3=Péché |first3=Sandrine |date=2009 |title=Poisson convergence for the largest eigenvalues of heavy tailed random matrices |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/AIHPB_2009__45_3_589_0/ |journal=  Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré, Probabilités et Statistiques|language=en |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=589–610 |doi=10.1214/08-AIHP188 |bibcode=2009AIHPB..45..589A |issn=1778-7017|arxiv=0710.3132 }}</ref>

==Functional forms==

=== Fredholm determinant ===
<math>F_2</math> can be given as the [[Fredholm determinant]]

:<math>F_2(s) = \det(I - A_s) = 1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n!} \int_{(s, \infty)^n} \det_{i, j = 1, ..., n}[A_s(x_i, x_j)]dx_1\cdots dx_n</math>

of the [[Integral transform|kernel]] <math>A_s</math> ("Airy kernel") on square integrable functions on the half line <math>(s,\infty)</math>, given in terms of [[Airy function]]s Ai by

:<math>A_s(x, y) = \begin{cases}
\frac{\mathrm{Ai}(x)\mathrm{Ai}'(y) - \mathrm{Ai}'(x)\mathrm{Ai}(y)}{x-y} \quad \text{if }x\neq y \\

\operatorname{Ai}' (x)^2- x (\operatorname{Ai}(x))^2 \quad \text{if }x=y
\end{cases}</math>

=== Painlevé transcendents ===
<math>F_2</math> can also be given as an integral

:<math>F_2(s) = \exp\left(-\int_s^\infty (x-s)q^2(x)\,dx\right)</math>

in terms of a solution<ref group="note">called "Hastings–McLeod solution". Published by

Hastings, S.P., McLeod, J.B.: A boundary value problem associated with the second Painlevé transcendent and the Korteweg-de Vries equation. Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. '''73''', 31–51 (1980)</ref> of a [[Painlevé equation]] of type II

:<math>q^{\prime\prime}(s) = sq(s)+2q(s)^3\,</math>
with boundary condition <math display="inline">\displaystyle q(s) \sim \textrm{Ai}(s), s\to\infty.</math> This function <math>q</math> is a [[Painlevé transcendent]].

Other distributions are also expressible in terms of the same <math>q</math>:{{sfnp|Tracy|Widom|1996}}
:<math>\begin{align}
F_1(s) &=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\int_s^\infty q(x)\,dx\right)\, \left(F_2(s)\right)^{1/2} \\
F_4(s/\sqrt{2}) &=\cosh\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_s^\infty q(x)\, dx\right)\, \left(F_2(s)\right)^{1/2}.

\end{align}</math>

=== Functional equations ===
Define <math display="block">\begin{align}
F(x) &= \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\int_{x}^{\infty}(y-x)q(y)^{2}\,d y\right) \\
E(x) &= \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\int_{x}^{\infty}q(y)\,d y\right)
\end{align}

</math>then<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">F_1(x) = E(x)F(x), \quad F_2(x) = F(x)^2, \quad \quad F_4\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(E(x) + \frac{1}{E(x)}\right)F(x)

</math>

== Occurrences ==
Other than in random matrix theory, the Tracy–Widom distributions occur in many other probability problems.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Majumdar |first1=Satya N |last2=Schehr |first2=Grégory |date=2014-01-31 |title=Top eigenvalue of a random matrix: large deviations and third order phase transition |journal=Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment |volume=2014 |issue=1 |page=01012 |doi=10.1088/1742-5468/2014/01/p01012 |arxiv=1311.0580 |bibcode=2014JSMTE..01..012M |s2cid=119122520 |issn=1742-5468}}</ref>

Let <math>l_n</math> be the length of the [[longest increasing subsequence]] in a random permutation sampled uniformly from <math>S_n</math>, the [[permutation group]] on n elements. Then the cumulative distribution function of <math>\frac{l_n - 2n^{1/2}}{n^{1/6}}</math> converges to <math>F_2</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Baik|Deift|Johansson|1999}}</ref>

== Third-order phase transition ==
The Tracy–Widom distribution exhibits a third-order [[phase transition]] in the large deviation behavior of the largest eigenvalue of a random matrix. This transition occurs at the edge of the [[Wigner semicircle distribution]], where the probability density of the largest eigenvalue follows distinct scaling laws depending on whether it deviates to the left or right of the edge.

Let <math>\Phi(w)</math> denote the rate function governing the large deviations of the largest eigenvalue <math>\lambda_{\max}</math>. For a Gaussian unitary ensemble, the probability density function of <math>\lambda_{\max}</math> satisfies, for large <math>N</math>,

:<math>P(\lambda_{\max} = w) \approx \exp \left( -\beta N^p \Phi(w) \right),</math>

where <math>p = 2</math> for deviations to the left of the spectral edge and <math>p = 1</math> for deviations to the right. When the small-deviation parts of the probability density are included, we have<math display="block">P\left(\lambda_{\max }=w, N\right) \approx \begin{cases}\exp \left[-\beta N^2 \Phi_{-}(w)\right] & , w<\sqrt{2} \&|w-\sqrt{2}| \sim \mathcal{O}(1) \\ \sqrt{2} N^{\frac{2}{3}} \mathcal{F}_\beta^{\prime}\left(\sqrt{2} N^{\frac{2}{3}}(w-\sqrt{2})\right) & , \\ \exp \left[-\beta N \Phi_{+}(w)\right] & , w>\sqrt{2} \&|w-\sqrt{2}| \sim \mathcal{O}\left(N^{-\frac{2}{3}}\right)\end{cases}</math>
[[File:Rate function of Tracy–Widom large deviation.svg|thumb|Rate function of the Tracy–Widom large deviation, and its leading approximation near the critical point.]]
The rate function <math>\Phi(w)</math> is given by separate expressions for <math>w < \sqrt{2}</math> and <math>w > \sqrt{2}</math>. <math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{-}(w)= & \frac{1}{108}\left[36 w^2-w^4-\left(15 w+w^3\right) \sqrt{w^2+6}\right. \\
& \left.+27\left(\ln 18-2 \ln \left(w+\sqrt{w^2+6}\right)\right)\right], w<\sqrt{2} .
\end{aligned}  </math>

<math display="block">\Phi_{+}(w)=\frac{1}{2} w \sqrt{w^2-2}+\ln \left[\frac{w-\sqrt{w^2-2}}{\sqrt{2}}\right]</math>

Near the critical point <math>w = \sqrt{2}</math>, the leading order behavior is

:<math>\Phi_-(w) \sim \frac{1}{6\sqrt{2}} (\sqrt{2} - w)^3, \quad w \to \sqrt{2}^-.  </math>

:<math>\Phi_+(w) \sim \frac{2^{7/4}}{3} (w - \sqrt{2})^{3/2}, \quad w \to \sqrt{2}^+.</math>

The third derivative of <math>\Phi(w)</math> is discontinuous at <math>w = \sqrt{2}</math>, which classifies this as a third-order phase transition. This type of transition is analogous to the [[Gross-Witten-Wadia phase transition]] in lattice gauge theory and the [[Douglas-Kazakov phase transition]] in two-dimensional [[quantum chromodynamics]]. The discontinuity in the third derivative of the free energy marks a fundamental change in the behavior of the system, where fluctuations transition between different scaling regimes.

This third-order transition has also been observed in problems related to the maximal height of non-intersecting Brownian excursions, conductance fluctuations in mesoscopic systems, and entanglement entropy in random pure states.<ref name=":1" />

To interpret this as a third-order transition in statistical mechanics, define the (generalized) free energy density of the system as<math display="block">
\mathcal{F}(w)=-\frac{1}{N^2} \ln P\left(\lambda_{\max }=w, N\right)
</math>then at the <math>N \to \infty</math> limit, <math>\mathcal{F}(w) = \begin{cases} \Phi_-(w) & w < \sqrt 2 \\ 0  & w > \sqrt 2 \end{cases} </math> has continuous first and second derivatives at the critical point <math>
w = \sqrt{2}
</math>, but a discontinuous third derivative.

The <math>-\ln P \propto N^2</math> lower end can be interpreted as the strongly interacting regime, where <math>N</math> objects are interacting strongly pairwise, so the total energy is proportional to <math>N^2</math>. The <math>-\ln P \propto N</math> upper end can be interpreted as the weakly interacting regime, where the objects are basically not interacting, so the total energy is proportional to <math>N</math>. The Tracy–Widom distribution phase transition then occurs at the point as the system switches from strongly to weakly interacting.

=== Coulomb gas model ===
[[File:Coulomb Gas distribution for various wall positions.svg|thumb|Coulomb Gas distribution for various wall positions.]]
This can be visualized in the [[Coulomb gas]] model by considering a gas of electric charges in a <math>V(x) = \frac 12 x^2</math> potential well. The distribution of the charges is the same as the distribution of the matrix eigenvalues. This gives the Wigner semi-circle law. To find the distribution of the largest eigenvalue, we take a wall and push against the Coulomb gas. If the wall is above <math>+\sqrt 2</math>, then most of the gas remains unaffected, and we are in the weak interaction regime. If the wall is below <math>+\sqrt 2</math>, then the entire bulk of the Coulomb gas is affected, and we are in the strong interaction regime.

The minimal Coulomb gas distribution is explicitly solvable as<math display="block">\rho_w^*(\lambda)= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{\pi} \sqrt{2-\lambda^2}, \quad \text { with } \quad-\sqrt{2} \leq \lambda \leq \sqrt{2} & \text { for } w>\sqrt{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{\lambda+L(w)}}{2 \pi \sqrt{w-\lambda}}[w+L(w)-2 \lambda] \quad \text { with } \quad-L(w) \leq \lambda \leq w & \text { for } w<\sqrt{2}\end{cases}</math>where <math>w</math> is the position of the wall, and <math>L(w)=\frac{2 \sqrt{w^2+6}-w}{3}</math>.

== Asymptotics ==

=== Probability density function ===
Let <math>f_\beta(x) = F_\beta'(x)</math> be the probability density function for the distribution, then<ref name=":1" /><math display="block">f_{\beta}(x) \sim \begin{cases}
e^{-\frac{\beta}{24}|x|^3}, \quad x \to -\infty\\
e^{-\frac{2\beta}{3}|x|^{3/2}},\quad x \to +\infty
\end{cases}</math>In particular, we see that it is severely skewed to the right: it is much more likely for <math>\lambda_{\max}</math> to be much larger than <math>2\sigma\sqrt{N}</math> than to be much smaller. This could be intuited by seeing that the limit distribution is the semicircle law, so there is "repulsion" from the bulk of the distribution, forcing <math>\lambda_{\max}</math> to be not much smaller than <math>2\sigma\sqrt{N}</math>.

At the <math>x\to -\infty</math> limit, a more precise expression is (equation 49 <ref name=":1" />)<math display="block">f_{\beta}(x) \sim \tau_{\beta}|x|^{(\beta^{2}+4-6\beta)/16\beta}\exp\left[-\beta\frac{|x|^{3}}{24}+\sqrt{2}\frac{\beta-2}{6}|x|^{3/2}\right]</math>for some positive number <math>\tau_\beta</math> that depends on <math>\beta</math>.

=== Cumulative distribution function ===
At the <math>x\to +\infty</math> limit,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baik |first1=Jinho |last2=Buckingham |first2=Robert |last3=DiFranco |first3=Jeffery |date=2008-02-26 |title=Asymptotics of Tracy-Widom Distributions and the Total Integral of a Painlevé II Function |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=280 |issue=2 |pages=463–497 |doi=10.1007/s00220-008-0433-5 |arxiv=0704.3636 |bibcode=2008CMaPh.280..463B |s2cid=16324715 |issn=0010-3616}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{align}

F(x)&=1-\frac{e^{-\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2}}}{32\pi x^{3/2}}\biggl(1-\frac{35}{24x^{3/2}}+{\cal O}(x^{-3})\biggr), \\

E(x) &=1-\frac{e^{-\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}}}{4\sqrt{\pi}x^{3/2}}\biggl(1-\frac{41}{48x^{3/2}}+{\cal O}(x^{-3})\biggr)
\end{align}</math>and at the <math>x\to -\infty</math> limit,<math display="block">\begin{align}
F(x)&=2^{1/48}e^{\frac{1}{2}\zeta^{\prime}(-1)}\frac{e^{-\frac{1}{24}|x|^{3}}}{|x|^{1/16}} \left(1+\frac{3}{2^{7}|x|^{3}}+O(|x|^{-6})\right) \\
E(x)&=\frac{1}{2^{1/4}}e^{-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}|x|^{3/2}} \Biggl(1-\frac{1}{24\sqrt{2}|x|^{3/2}}+{\cal O}(|x|^{-3})\Biggr).
\end{align}</math>where <math>\zeta</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]], and <math>\zeta' (-1) = -0.1654211437</math>.

This allows derivation of <math>x\to \pm\infty</math> behavior of <math>F_\beta</math>. For example,<math display="block">\begin{align}

1-F_{2}(x)&=\frac{1}{32\pi x^{3/2}}e^{-4x^{3/2}/3}(1+O(x^{-3/2})),
\\
F_{2}(-x)&=\frac{2^{1/24}e^{\zeta^{\prime}(-1)}}{x^{1/8}}e^{-x^{3}/12}\biggl(1+\frac{3}{2^{6}x^{3}}+O(x^{-6})\biggr).

\end{align}</math>

=== Painlevé transcendent ===

The Painlevé transcendent has asymptotic expansion at <math>x \to -\infty</math> (equation 4.1 of <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tracy |first1=Craig A. |last2=Widom |first2=Harold |date=May 1993 |title=Level-spacing distributions and the Airy kernel |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=305 |issue=1–2 |pages=115–118 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(93)91114-3 |arxiv=hep-th/9210074 |bibcode=1993PhLB..305..115T |s2cid=13912236 |issn=0370-2693}}</ref>)<math display="block">q(x) = \sqrt{-\frac{x}{2}} \left(1 + \frac 18 x^{-3} - \frac{73}{128} x^{-6} + \frac{10657}{1024}x^{-9} + O(x^{-12})\right)</math>This is necessary for numerical computations, as the <math>q\sim \sqrt{-x/2}</math> solution is unstable: any deviation from it tends to drop it to the <math>q \sim -\sqrt{-x/2}</math> branch instead.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bender |first1=Carl M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-yQXwhE6iWMC&dq=Advanced+Mathematical+Methods+for+Scientists+and+Engineers&pg=PR13 |title=Advanced Mathematical Methods for Scientists and Engineers I: Asymptotic Methods and Perturbation Theory |last2=Orszag |first2=Steven A. |date=1999-10-29 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-98931-0 |pages=163–165 |language=en}}</ref>

==Numerics==

Numerical techniques for obtaining numerical solutions to the Painlevé equations of the types II and V, and numerically evaluating eigenvalue distributions of random matrices in the beta-ensembles were first presented by {{harvtxt|Edelman|Persson|2005}} using [[MATLAB]]. These approximation techniques were further analytically justified in {{harvtxt|Bejan|2005}} and used to provide numerical evaluation of Painlevé II and Tracy–Widom distributions (for <math>\beta=1,2,4</math>) in [[S-PLUS]]. These distributions have been tabulated in {{harvtxt|Bejan|2005}} to four significant digits for values of the argument in increments of 0.01; a statistical table for p-values was also given in this work. {{harvtxt|Bornemann|2010}} gave accurate and fast algorithms for the numerical evaluation of <math>F_\beta</math> and the density functions 
<math>f_\beta(s)=dF_\beta/ds</math> for <math>\beta=1,2,4</math>.  These algorithms can be used to compute numerically the [[mean]], [[variance]], [[skewness]] and [[excess kurtosis]] of the distributions <math>F_\beta</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Su |first1=Zhong-gen |last2=Lei |first2=Yu-huan |last3=Shen |first3=Tian |date=2021-03-01 |title=Tracy-Widom distribution, Airy2 process and its sample path properties |journal=Applied Mathematics-A Journal of Chinese Universities |language=en |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=128–158 |doi=10.1007/s11766-021-4251-2 |s2cid=237903590 |issn=1993-0445|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Functions for working with the Tracy–Widom laws are also presented in the R package 'RMTstat' by {{harvtxt|Johnstone|Ma|Perry|Shahram|2009}} and MATLAB package 'RMLab' by {{harvtxt|Dieng|2006}}.

For a simple approximation based on a shifted gamma distribution see {{harvtxt|Chiani|2014}}.

{{Harvtxt|Shen|Serkh|2022}} developed a spectral algorithm for the eigendecomposition of the integral operator <math>A_s</math>, which can be used to rapidly evaluate Tracy–Widom distributions, or, more generally, the distributions of the <math>k</math>th largest level at the soft edge scaling limit of Gaussian ensembles, to machine accuracy.

== Tracy-Widom and KPZ universality ==
The Tracy–Widom distribution appears as a limit distribution in the universality class of the [[KPZ equation]]. For example it appears under <math>t^{1/3}</math> scaling of the one-dimensional [[KPZ equation]] with fixed time.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Gideon |last1=Amir |first2=Ivan |last2=Corwin |first3=Jeremy |last3=Quastel |publisher=Wiley |title=Probability distribution of the free energy of the continuum directed random polymer in 1 + 1 dimensions |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |volume=64 |number=4 |date=2010 |pages=466–537 |doi=10.1002/cpa.20347|arxiv=1003.0443 }}</ref>
